scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Aleke developed in the 1950s within the Maroon communities of eastern Suriname.
It is a modern genre that evolved from traditional Ndjuka (Aukan) music.

The genre is noted for being a more recent development compared to older forms like awasa, reflecting the modernization of Maroon culture as communities interacted more frequently with urban environments and modern technology.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Aleke is primarily a genre of entertainment and social expression.
It is played at festivities and public gatherings.
Unlike older religious forms, Aleke lyrics often focus on social commentary, daily life, and modern experiences, making it a vital part of contemporary Maroon identity.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is a high-energy social form.
While specific technical steps are not detailed in the sources, it is described as a 'popular' and 'danceable' genre that evolved from rhythmic music.
It involves responding to the fast-paced, complex drumming typical of Maroon percussion styles.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is characterized by a fast tempo and complex percussion.
Instruments include traditional Maroon drums, often supplemented by kawina-style double-skinned drums.
Listen for the Double-skinned drums, Electric guitar, Bass guitar, Keyboards.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 120 beats a minute.
A high-speed blend of traditional Maroon drumming and modern electric instruments, featuring a prominent lead singer answered by a unison chorus.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Aleke is performed in both traditional Maroon villages in the Surinamese interior and in urban settings like Paramaribo.
Costumes for social dancing are typically contemporary everyday wear, though performance groups may wear traditional Maroon textiles like the pangi.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The genre is associated with the Ndjuka (Aukan) people of eastern Suriname.
While specific individual performers are not listed in the sources, the genre is recognized as a major popular form alongside kaseko and kawina.
Aleke is specific to the Maroon communities, particularly the Ndjuka.
Aleke is a descendant of traditional Maroon drumming and singing styles. it is a sibling to other Maroon genres like seketi and has been influenced by the instrumentation of kaseko and kawina.
